analysis.one_liner: Blocks states from taxing businesses that sell into a state without a physical presence there.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote, dying in the House Judiciary Committee after one subcommittee hearing in February 2014.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1959, federal law has stopped states from taxing out-of-state companies that merely solicit sales of physical goods by mail or phone. This bill would dramatically expand that shield: it would cover sales of services, digital products, and other intangible transactions, extend the protection beyond income taxes to nearly all state business taxes, and bar states from taxing any out-of-state business unless it has employees, property, or an exclusive agent physically in the state. States could still collect sales and use taxes, but their main tools for taxing business activity conducted in their borders would be sharply cut back.
analysis.who_benefits: Multistate and remote businesses — including sellers of services, digital goods, streaming, and cloud products — that sell heavily into a state without maintaining offices, employees, or warehouses there. They would pay no state income, gross-receipts, or franchise taxes on those sales no matter how large their in-state customer base.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the 1959 federal shield (Public Law 86-272), which currently protects only solicitation of sales of tangible personal property, to 'all other forms of property, services, and other transactions,' fulfilled or distributed from outside the state.

Prohibits any state from imposing a net income tax or any other business activity tax on a person who lacks physical presence in the state, defined narrowly as having employees there, owning or leasing property there, or using a non-employee agent working exclusively for that business — and treats fewer than 15 days of presence as too small to count.

Extends these protections beyond net income taxes to every other 'business activity tax,' such as gross-receipts and franchise taxes, for tax periods beginning on or after January 1, 2014, while expressly excluding sales and use taxes.
Protects the activities of independent contractors — soliciting, selling, furnishing information, even maintaining an office — from creating tax liability for the company that hired them.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which would lose tax revenue from companies selling into their states with no physical footprint. To make up the difference, states would have to raise taxes on residents and businesses that do have a physical presence in state, or cut services. In-state businesses would bear a relatively heavier share of the tax load than remote competitors.

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip states of their main tools for taxing business activity conducted within their borders, cutting revenue that funds schools, roads, and other services residents rely on, and shifting the burden onto taxpayers and businesses that are physically present.

It would place in-state businesses at a competitive disadvantage: a company shipping into the state from elsewhere would owe nothing on its in-state sales, while a local rival paying rent and employing residents would be fully taxed on the same transactions.

By extending the shield to services and digital transactions and to all business activity taxes, the bill would go far beyond the narrow 1959 compromise covering catalog and mail-order sellers, reaching a modern economy of streaming, software, and cloud services that the original law never contemplated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to a specific set of businesses — remote and multistate sellers that want to sell into states without being taxed there — while the cost falls broadly on everyone who depends on state-funded services. The bill does carve out sales and use taxes and preserves state authority to combat sham transactions and require combined reporting, but those limits do not change the basic transfer: tax burden moves from out-of-state sellers to in-state businesses and residents.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee for the rest of the Congress: it was referred to a subcommittee, got one hearing in February 2014, and never received a markup or a vote in the full House before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI) introduced the Business Activity Tax Simplification Act of 2013 on August 2, 2013, with 12 cosponsors (10 Republicans, 2 Democrats).

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and on September 13, 2013 was referred further to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
The subcommittee held a hearing on February 26, 2014 — the only committee action of record on the bill.
The full Judiciary Committee never reported the bill and the House never voted on it; no further action appears before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments kept their existing authority to tax out-of-state businesses, and the multistate sellers that would have gained a broad federal tax shield got nothing. Ordinary taxpayers were spared a revenue shift onto in-state businesses and residents.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State treasuries, which kept their taxing authority

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a small bipartisan group of cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.role: Chair, House Judiciary Committee; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as one of its eight original backers; the committee he chaired took no further action on it beyond a subcommittee hearing.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never reported it to the full House, leaving it without a markup or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: State governments and state tax administrators
against.role: States whose business tax revenue the bill would have restricted
against.what_they_did: State tax officials have long opposed federal legislation imposing a strict physical-presence limit on state business taxes, arguing it would cost states revenue and tilt the field against in-state firms.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was mostly Republican (10 of 12) with two Democrats, but no vote was ever recorded, so the chamber's actual partisan divide is unknown.

industries.industry: Remote sellers and multistate businesses (including digital services, streaming, and cloud providers)
industries.note: The bill would let them sell into any state — even heavily — without paying that state's income or business activity taxes, as long as they have no employees or property there. The lost revenue would come from state budgets that fund services everyone uses, and from in-state competitors who would keep paying.

The bill would bar states from taxing out-of-state companies lacking physical presence and would extend that bar to nearly all business activity taxes, shrinking state revenue and forcing higher taxes on residents or cuts to services.

They benefit relatively from the bill's death — they keep paying state business taxes while remote rivals would have been shielded. Had the bill passed, in-state firms would have borne a heavier relative tax burden than out-of-state competitors.
